wa_bouldering_at_index.blurb: Boulder problems scattered through the forest around the town of Index, below the town's big cliffs, across the North Fork of the Skykomish River and along the river to the west. Every climb here is a boulder problem, from easy V0 slabs through a deep middle band at V1 to V5, up to a handful of V10 and harder testpieces. The rock is fine-grained granite, and the movement leans toward thin edges, small crimps, balance and careful footwork rather than raw power. River Boulders, Sasquatch Boulders and Zelda Boulders hold the largest clusters. Fall brings the stickiest friction; spring is cool but often damp, summer is dry and best early or late in the day, and winter is hit or miss with snow and ice.

az_granite_gardens.blurb: Part of the Granite Dells, a landscape of rounded desert granite just north and east of Prescott in central Arizona, at around 5,000 feet. The stone is medium-grained and a little grainy in places. Trad leads outnumber sport routes by roughly two to one, and a few top ropes and boulder problems round things out. Grades run from easy up to 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.7 to 5.11 range and the busiest stretch around 5.10 and 5.11, so there is plenty for strong climbers and a fair share of moderates. Two main sub-areas hold almost everything: the High Rappel Area, the larger one, and The Oasis, with The Waning Wall a small extra.

ma_quincy_quarries.blurb: A set of old granite quarries in Quincy, southeast of Boston, with at least twenty faces and craglets lettered by wall. Top-roping dominates, followed by a good number of trad lines, some boulder problems and only a few sport routes. Grades run from easy to 5.12, with most climbs between 5.5 and 5.10, so beginners and intermediates are well served. Walls reach up to about 90 feet, but most top ropes are well under 50. Slab and vertical face climbing on small holds is the norm, and spray paint covers much of the rock, making the lower sections notably slick. C Wall, M Wall and Swingles Quarry are among the larger walls. Many lines are short and squeezed together, with variations.

nt_yellowknife.blurb: A small handful of crags and boulders in and around the capital of the Northwest Territories. Bouldering makes up most of the climbing, mainly at the easy end, with plenty of V0 to V2 problems and a thinner tail of harder ones up to V5. Roped climbing is a minority, split between sport, trad and top rope, running from 5.5 to the low 5.12s with most in the 5.8 to 5.11 range, plus a few ice lines. The outdoor season is short, from about mid-May to early October, under fairly mild, dry weather. Cameron Falls and Hidden Lake Territorial Park is the biggest zone, followed by The Ravine, with Frame Lake and Tin Can Hill next in size.

wv_furnace_road_areas.blurb: A cluster of boulder fields inside Coopers Rock State Forest in northern West Virginia, almost entirely bouldering with only a stray rope route or two. The forest's boulders are a coarse, quartz-rich sandstone with a gritty feel: expect slopers, rounded holds and shallow features, and a reputation for stiff grades. Difficulty runs from easy warm-ups through a deep middle of V3 to V7, then thins out toward the V10 range. Greenbrier Boulders is the biggest pocket, followed by Wonderland Ridge, a quieter ridgeline of spread-out problems among laurel and rhododendron, and Eldorado. Smaller groups such as Fat Rat Boulders and Prize Fighter Roof fill in the rest. The rock is slow to dry after hard rain, so plan around the weather.
